AWARD/JUDGMENT FACTUAL POSITION & PLEADINGS 1.

This petition was filed U/s 166 r/w Section 140 of MV Act 1988 for grant of compensation in respect of the grievous injureis sustained by the petitioner in a road traffic accident which took place at 03.00 PM on 16/06/2015 at a spot situated on GT Road, near Garhi Kalan falling within the jurisdiction of PS Gannaur, District Sonepat, Haryana.

As per petition, at the relevant time, the petitioner and some others were travelling in a car bearing registration number DL8CV4329 from Panipat to their Village Salarpur Majra, which was being driven by her son namely Prabhat.
When the said vehicle reached at the spot of accident, it dashed into the rear of a parked Truck bearing registration number HR731328 (hereinafter referred to as "offending vehicle'').
Driver of the vehicle bearing registration no. DL8CV4329, i.e. the son of the petitioner herein, succumbed at the spot.
Driver of the offending vehicle (R1) fled from the spot after a while.
Petitioner claims that the accident occured as the driver of the offending vehicle had parked his vehicle in the middle of the road (on GT Road)

Petitioner claims that she has sustained grievous injuries including multiple fractures in the accident and has incurred expenses to the tune of Rs. 5 Lakhs towards medical treatment.
Petitioner further claims that at the relevant time, she was 54 years and was earning a sum of Rs. 14,000/ per month from her vocation of sewing and stitching.
She seeks compensation to the tune of Rs. 30 Lakhs on account of the injuries sustained in the accident.
R1 is the driver of the offending vehicle.
R2 is the owner of the offending vehicle.
R3 is the insurer of the offending vehicle.
Presence of all the parties was secured.
All the respondents were directed to file their Written Statements.

sentences.text: Pages No. 10/28 LOVLEEN 2023.04.18 conducted by an accident tribunal is similar to that followed by a civil court and in civil matters the facts are required to be established by preponderance of probabilities only and not by strict rules of evidence or beyond reasonable doubts as are required in a criminal prosecution.

The burden of proof in a civil case is never as heavy as that is required in a criminal case, but in a claim petition under the Motor Vehicles Act, this burden is infact even lesser than that in a civil case.

Reference in this regard can be made to the propositions of law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bimla Devi and others Vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation and others, reported in (2009) 13 SC 530, which were reiterated in the subsequent judgment in the case of Parmeshwari Vs. Amir Chand and others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 (Civil Appeal No.1082 of 2011) and also recently in another case Mangla Ram Vs. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. & Ors., 2018 Law Suit (SC) 303.

PW1 further deposes in her affidavit that at the relevant time the offending vehicle was parked in the middle of the road.

Although the said assertion has been denied by R1 & R2 in their joint written statement but they have not bothered to explain as to 'where' on the GT Road the offending vehicle was parked at the relevant time.
It is only R3 which asserts (contrary to the assertion of PW1) that the offending vehicle was parked on the left side of the road.
Perusal of the certified copies of the criminal court records reveal that a site plan was prepared by the police during the investigation in the relevant FIR.
Although the said site plan is devoid of any measurements but still the same seems to reflect that the accident took place on the left side of the road/carriage way from Panipat to Delhi.

Consequently, it could be safely assumed that at the relevant the offending vehicle was parked on the left side of the road and not in the middle of the road as has been deposed by PW1.
11.
It is apparent from the above that the vehicle bearing registration no. DL8CV4329 dashed into the rear of the offending vehicle which was parked on the left side of the GT Road.
Now we may take up the question of rashness and negligence.
Admittedly, the accident took place at about 03.00 PM on 16/06/2015.
In the absence of any averment on the part of petitioner as to lack of visibility due to weather or otherwise, this Tribunal MACT No. 1003/18 Sumitra Devi Vs.
Avtar Sing & Ors

. Pages No. 12/28 LOVLEEN 2023.04.18 is constrained to hold that the driver of the vehicle bearing registration no. DL8CV4329 was not diligent while driving his vehicle as he dashed his vehicle into the rear of the offending vehicle in broad day light.
However, R 1 could not be absolved completely.
Here we may cite the Rules of the Road Regulations, 1989 which prohibit the parking of any vehicle on a main road or one carrying fast traffic (Rule 15).

Parking the offending vehicle on GT Road in violation of the rules without any reasonable cause reflect that R1 was grossly negligent and whose misconduct is one of the factors which lead to the occurrence of the accident in question.

In the given facts and circumstances, this Tribunal holds that the accident in question took place on account of negligence of the driver of the vehicle bearing registration no. DL8CV4329 as well as R1 (driver of offending vehicle) and both are equally to be blamed for the occurrence of the accident.
12. It is not disputed that the petitioner has sustained grievous injuries including multiple fractures in the above accident.
She has also sustained disability to the extent of 50% with respect to her left upper limb and left lower limb due to injuries sustained in the above accident.
13. Accordingly, this issue stands decided in favour of the petitioner.

As the issue no.1 has been proved in affirmative and in favour of the petitioner, the petitioner has become entitled to be compensated for the injuries suffered in the above accident, but the computation of compensation and liability to pay the same are required to be decided.
15. In terms of provisions contained in Section 168 of the MV Act the compensation which is to be awarded by this tribunal is required to be 'just'.
In the injury cases a claimant is entitled to two different kinds of compensations i.e. pecuniary as well as nonpecuniary damages.

The pecuniary damages or special damages are those damages which are awarded and designed to make good the losses which are capable of being calculated in terms of money and the object of awarding these damages is to indemnify the claimant for the expenses which he had already incurred or is likely to incur in respect of the injuries suffered by him in the accident.
The nonpecuniary or general damages are those damages which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations.

The pecuniary or special damages generally include the expenses incurred by the claimant towards his treatment, special diet, conveyance, cost of nursing/ attendant, loss of income/earning capacity etc.
and the nonpecuniary damages generally include the compensation for the mental or physical shock, pain and sufferings, loss of amenities of life, marriage prospects and disfiguration etc.
The above categories falling under both the heads of compensation are not exhaustive in nature but only illustrative.
It is also necessary to state here MACT No. 1003/18 Sumitra Devi Vs. Avtar Sing & Ors.

that no amount of money or compensation can put the injured/claimant exactly in the same position or place where he was before the accident and an effort is to be made only to reasonably compensate him or to put him almost in the same place or position where he could have been if the alleged accident had not taken place and this compensation is to be assessed in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.
The object of compensating him is also not to reward him or to make him rich in an unjust manner.

It is also well settled that the 'just' compensation to be awarded to the claimant has to be calculated objectively and it may involve some guess work in calculating the different amounts which the claimant may be entitled under the different heads of compensation.

Reference in this regard can be made on some of important judgments on the subject like the judgment in the case of R.D. Hattangadi Vs. Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd., AIR 1995 SC 755, Arvind Kumar Mishra Vs. New India Assurance Company Limited, (2010) 10 SCC 254 and Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Anr., (2011) 1 SCC 343.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
It is well settled that the procedure followed for proceedings MACT No. 1003/18 Sumitra Devi Vs.
Avtar Sing & Ors.
The burden of proof in a civil case is never as heavy as that is required in a criminal case, but in a claim petition under the Motor Vehicles Act, this burden is infact even lesser than that in a civil case.
Reference in this regard can be made to the propositions of law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bimla Devi and others Vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation and others, reported in (2009) 13 SC 530, which were reiterated in the subsequent judgment in the case of Parmeshwari Vs. Amir Chand and others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 (Civil Appeal No.1082 of 2011) and also recently in another case Mangla Ram Vs. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. & Ors., 2018 Law Suit (SC) 303.
9.
Accordingly, this Tribunal has no hesitation to hold that the vehicle bearing registration no. DL8CV4329, in which the MACT No. 1003/18 Sumitra Devi Vs. Avtar Sing & Ors.
Perusal of the certified copies of the criminal court records reveal that a site plan was prepared by the police during the investigation in the relevant FIR.
Although the said site plan is devoid of any measurements but still the same seems to reflect that the accident took place on the left side of the road/carriage way from Panipat to Delhi.
Consequently, it could be safely assumed that at the relevant the offending vehicle was parked on the left side of the road and not in the middle of the road as has been deposed by PW1.
11.
It is apparent from the above that the vehicle bearing registration no. DL8CV4329 dashed into the rear of the offending vehicle which was parked on the left side of the GT Road.
However, R 1 could not be absolved completely.
Parking the offending vehicle on GT Road in violation of the rules without any reasonable cause reflect that R1 was grossly negligent and whose misconduct is one of the factors which lead to the occurrence of the accident in question.
In the given facts and circumstances, this Tribunal holds that the accident in question took place on account of negligence of the driver of the vehicle bearing registration no. DL8CV4329 as well as R1 (driver of offending vehicle) and both are equally to be blamed for the occurrence of the accident.
In the injury cases a claimant is entitled to two different kinds of compensations i.e. pecuniary as well as nonpecuniary damages.
The pecuniary damages or special damages are those damages which are awarded and designed to make good the losses which are capable of being calculated in terms of money and the object of awarding these damages is to indemnify the claimant for the expenses which he had already incurred or is likely to incur in respect of the injuries suffered by him in the accident.
The nonpecuniary or general damages are those damages which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations.
The pecuniary or special damages generally include the expenses incurred by the claimant towards his treatment, special diet, conveyance, cost of nursing/ attendant, loss of income/earning capacity etc.
and the nonpecuniary damages generally include the compensation for the mental or physical shock, pain and sufferings, loss of amenities of life, marriage prospects and disfiguration etc.
Pages No. 14/28 LOVLEEN Date:
that no amount of money or compensation can put the injured/claimant exactly in the same position or place where he was before the accident and an effort is to be made only to reasonably compensate him or to put him almost in the same place or position where he could have been if the alleged accident had not taken place and this compensation is to be assessed in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.
The object of compensating him is also not to reward him or to make him rich in an unjust manner.
It is also well settled that the 'just' compensation to be awarded to the claimant has to be calculated objectively and it may involve some guess work in calculating the different amounts which the claimant may be entitled under the different heads of compensation.
Reference in this regard can be made on some of important judgments on the subject like the judgment in the case of R.D. Hattangadi Vs. Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd., AIR 1995 SC 755, Arvind Kumar Mishra Vs. New India Assurance Company Limited, (2010) 10 SCC 254 and Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Anr., (2011) 1 SCC 343.
16.
Given the advanced age of petitioner (i.e. 65 years) at the time of above accident (as per Aadhar Card Ex. PW1/1 petitioner was born on 11/09/1950), it is difficult to assume that petitioner could engage in the commercial activity of stitching or sewing, as the said tasks are labour intensive and require a high degree of concentration and fitness.
Hence, keeping in view the extent and nature of the injuries suffered by petitioner and duration of the treatment taken by her etc., an amount of Rs. 1,00,000/ is being awarded to her towards pain and sufferings during the said period of her treatment and immobility.
Apparently, the present case is one involving composite negligence of drivers of the offending vehicle as well as the vehicle bearing registration no. DL8CU4329.
Since the offending vehicle was insured with R3 at the time of accident, therefore, R3 is liable to indemnify R2 in respect of above liability.
